utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have today's appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution, together with my colleagues, Barney Thomas, Ms. April Carter, and our case manager, Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We are at the stage where we'd like to hear the statement by Mr. Perisic. Mr. Perisic, will you please make your statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphone is not on for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The microphone may not be on, but the accused should be able to hear without his microphone on. If the interpretation is not getting through, it comes through his ears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only hear the voice in English. I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perisic. Just hold on. Let's see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perisic. You may proceed with your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that the indictment against me is unique in the history of international law of war. I'm not receiving any interpretation, anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perisic, you are speaking, so you will not receive any interpretation. You will be interpreted to us who do not understand your language. Only when we speak will you receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Okay. Fine. Yes, yes, I understand. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. Your Honours, I believe that the indictment against me is unique in the history of international law of war. Never before have a commander and the Chief Of Staff of General Staff of one army been criminally responsible for the crimes committed by members of the armed forces of another state or entity. I was born in Serbia during the Second World War. My wife is from Trnovo, that is the municipality of Sarajevo, which is now in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have two sons. One was born in Karlovac which is now in the state of Croatia; the other was born in Podgorica which is now in the state of Montenegro. The four of us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. Will you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. So, the four of us at the time when we were born, we were born in a single state, yet now we come from four different states. After I graduated from the military academy, I became an officer in a multi-ethnic army and a multi-ethnic state, and they remained thus until the end of my career. I, myself, have contributed to this, and this is something I'm really proud of. In my 32-year-long career, I served 27 years, 80 per cent of that time, in posts in Croatia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, not in the republic in which I was born. I was appointed the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army at the time when the situation was extremely complex in August 1993. In the neighbouring Croatia, there was a state between war and peace; and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which had recently seceded, the war was well on its way to escalation. As for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, it was in the throws of an unprecedented isolation, not only financial and material but also moral, legal, and political. At the time, the situation in the Yugoslav Army was even tougher. The existing legislation was completely outdated and there were no new laws in place yet. Families of the JNA personnel who had lived in the republics that had seceded before the war now came to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia utterly frustrated without any poverty -- on the brink of poverty. As the Chief of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, I was fully able to recognise the interests of the citizens and of the state; and I was ready, in order to implement those and protect those interests, to commit all I had, including my life. But I was also able to recognise or see a situation where the regime places its own interests above those of the state. That is why we were able to stop the war from spreading to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. We prevented the misuse of the Army of Yugoslavia, made it possible for the democratic forces and processes in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to develop, eliminated party politics from the Army of Yugoslavia, and turned it into the most highly respected institution in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. By its existence, the level of training and its treatment towards citizens, in particular those who were involved in demonstrations to protect the -- their will expressed at elections, the VJ instilled trust and, in fact, represented the most open and the most democratic institution in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is something that the representatives of students and other protesters' delegations always stressed whenever I received them at that time, and so did many representatives of the international community, including some Western heads of state. When the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in the deepest isolation, the Army of Yugoslavia organised two air shows with the participation of the air forces of France, Italy, Austria, Greece, Romania, Bulgaria, and the Russia Federation. The air shows were attended by more than 300.000 citizens. At that time, we mediated in the effort to achieve the release of the hostages from the peace-keeping forces, the international peace-keeping forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of the French pilots captured by the VRS personnel in the course of the NATO air strikes against Republika Srpska. This made it possible to sign the Dayton Agreement in Paris, and I hope that our French friends, in particular former President Chirac; and my colleague, the head of the Joint Chiefs of Staff of the French army, General Gourmelon, have not forgotten this. During this time, there was a very real danger for my removal from office, but I did not fear that. I feared that once I was out of the way, the VJ would be misused and that the war would spread in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to be more specific to Kosovo and Metohija. Unfortunately, subsequent events have proven those fears to be founded. I tried to exert some influence on the regime, avoiding a military coup; but when I realised that their decisions inevitably lead us into a conflict with NATO in October 1998, I went public with a warning about what was in store for us if we failed to comply with the provisions in the Resolution 1199 of the UN Security Council. That is why, because of this conduct, at its session held on the 24th of November, 1998, the Supreme Defence Council removed me from my post of the Chief of Staff of the VJ, despite the opposition of the President of Montenegro who was there as a member of the Supreme Defence Council. I was not present at the session. After my removal from office, I addressed the public saying, and I quote: "The current government does not want to have leaders with integrity, people who use their own heads." I was removed from my post of the Chief of the VJ General Staff illegally and without being consulted. I refused to accept the invented post of an advisor to the federal government, and I remained at the disposal of the army, the people, and the state." I never did accept any new post, and the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as the chairman of the Supreme Defence Council in March 1991, punished me by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- punished me by passing a decree discharging me from the Army of Yugoslavia ten years before the time that was stipulated without benefits I was entitled to. In August 1999, I founded the political party that was called the Movement for a Democratic Serbia. Together with the other democratic forces, we launched a political struggle to achieve -- to fight totalitarianism. That is why proceedings were instituted against me before the military court of honour. Although I was a civilian at the time, I was stripped of my rank. During the events of the 5th October, year 2000, I played a key role in the planning and implementation of the activities designed to give a creative shape to the energy of the millions of protesters to pressure the regime into recognising the will of the people in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia expressed at the elections, and this resulted in a resounding victory of the protesters without any casualties. After that I was elected into the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I was appointed the chairman of committee for defence and security in the FRY Assembly and deputy prime minister of Serbia. In that period, I took active part in the passing of the law on cooperation of Serbia and Montenegro with the International Tribunal in The Hague. On the 2nd of March, 2005, when the Serb government received the indictment, I made the following public statement. I quote: "I have received the indictment from the Tribunal in The Hague. I did what I always do when I find myself at a turning point. Without any outside influence, and acting in accordance with my own conscience, I decided to face the International Tribunal in The Hague. Crimes have no nationality, and that is why I believe that whoever and wherever committed crimes must be punished. That is why it is no dilemma for me. I will face any court, in particular the International Tribunal in The Hague, because it is the only way for me to defend my honour as an officer, the reputation of the army, and the dignity of my people." I came here and I reported to the Detention Unit on the 7th of March, 2005. Before the indictment was made public, I believed then, and I believe now, that you, Your Honours, after a fair, unbiased, and full consideration of the facts, the circumstances, and the reality of what I did and what really happened at the time, will reach a just decision. I regret deeply that there were victims of crimes in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. I sympathise deeply with the families of the victims. Every life lost in war is an irreplaceable loss for the society, but lives lost to crime are an even greater loss. I believe that all those who committed crimes will face trial and will receive proper punishment, and I hope that war crimes will never happen again. At my Initial Appearance before this Tribunal, I pleaded not guilty on all counts in the indictment; and now, again, I say to you, Your Honours, I am convinced that you will hear the arguments of both parties, without any prejudice, professionally and carefully, and will deliver a fair and honourable judgement. I hope that I will be allowed to present my case and to exercise all the rights that this Tribunal guarantees to me. Only the totality of evidence will make you able to understand my conduct, my role, my environment, my context. My defence will contribute to the determination of all the relevant facts, to challenge the allegations in the indictment and prove my innocence. After all, it is an obligation I have towards my profession, my family, and my army, my people, and my state. As a professional soldier, I hate war because I am fully aware of the fact that all wars, in particular the war that was waged in the former Yugoslavia - it was a civil war, a religious war, interethnic war - is the worst thing that can happen in a society. I have felt the horrors of war. I despise it because of the consequences it leaves in its wake, because of the lies it relies on, the hatred that it engenders, because it ushers in dictatorship to topple democracy, and because of the misery it leaves in its wake. Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perisic. I guess the parties would like us to discuss some of the issues before we call the first witness for the Prosecution. I've been given a list of topics that the parties would like us to discuss. There may, perhaps, be some items that the Chamber might also want to add. The four points that have been mentioned are, first of all, the guidelines, the proposed guidelines; proofing notes; protected witness issues; pending motions and recently filed motions. Have I got the issues from the parties correct, Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, with the addition that the Prosecution has one very brief additional housekeeping matter to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Would you like to add it now, or will you raise it later?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With your leave, I can add it now, Your Honour. It's simply to correct the -- some points on the record yesterday from Mr. Harmon's opening statement, where Mr. Harmon realised last evening that he had misspoken. I can explain that now or later, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just add it as an item and come to it at the relevant time, because I'm not quite sure whether the Defence would like to say something on that issue. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There would be one additional issue which may well deal specifically with the first witness that the Prosecution intends to call, and I sent an e-mail late last night to all parties. That deals with the enforcement of prior rulings in this case, as they could well affect present testimony, specifically the testimony of the first witness that the Prosecution intends to call; that is, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. I'm going to suggest that we just deal with the items as they follow seriatim. On the proposed guidelines, I believe, in addition to the suggestions that the parties had submitted earlier, there have been new ones coming up yesterday. Now, I haven't even seen those. I don't know whether Judge Picard and Judge David have seen them. Maybe the best way to deal with them is just for the parties to indicate what they are and what are the new things that were added last night. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, beginning at paragraph 1, the parties agreed to suggest to add a sentence at the end of paragraph 1, which is the paragraph titled "Order of Calling Witnesses." And the suggested last sentence, Your Honours, would be the following: "In the case of any witness in respect of whom 100 or more documents are intended to be used, the list of such documents is to be provided at least five days before the start of the testimony."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I ask, yes, Mr. Guy-Smith --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "Five working days," I should have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. "At least five working days before the start of the testimony." That's what it says. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith, is that what you wanted to correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For my own clarification, now, you're saying 100 documents; you're not saying 100 pages. Do I understand that I can give you 100 -- only when I give you 100 documents, irrespective of the number of pages, could each one of them could have 10.000 pages and you would need five working days?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the agreement that we have made with the Prosecution. We trust that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was there a meeting of minds on --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There actually was a meeting of minds on that issue, and we did take into account the potential dilemma with regard to defining it by number of documents as opposed to number of pages. However, we believe that the body of information that we have been supplied thus far, some of the documents which are hundreds of pages are documents that we will be conversant with by the time those witnesses come to the fore. So the only -- our expectation is that we won't be seeing too many more documents that run into hundreds or thousands - I don't think we'll get to thousands - but hundreds of pages under this particular plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I also trust that in the event there is a particularly large document, that the Prosecution, being aware of the difficulties that exist in terms of just getting through it, will give us more than what the minimum time is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you also will give them minimum time when their time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to be clear that the way that the document was studiously inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. We understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any other amendments? I guess it will be paragraph 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if you could turn to 15, please, the paragraph entitled "Length of Examination." After the first sentence, the parties agreed to suggest the following language be added: "Such a system shall record time used: (a) by the Prosecution for its examination-in-chief; (b) by the Defence for cross-examination; (c) by the Prosecution for re-examination; (d) by the Judges for putting questions to the witnesses; and (e) for all other matters, including procedural matters. Regular reports on the use of time shall be compiled by the Registry every two weeks for use by the Trial Chamber and the parties. Significant time spent dealing with objections will not be counted against the party then examining the witness. Where there are time savings (i.e., where direct examination takes less time than estimated) these may be apportioned by the examining party to other witnesses in its case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That would -- that is the suggested change for paragraph 15, Your Honour, that was agreed to by the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's paragraph 19, I guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The parties agreed to suggest in paragraph 19, entitled "92 bis Witnesses Appearing for Cross-Examination" that the first sentence of that paragraph should read: "Where a witness whose previous testimony or statement has been admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, has been called solely for the purposes of cross-examination, the calling party should not introduce new evidence through examination-in-chief, without leave of the Court." And it's those last five words that the parties have agreed to suggest to the Chamber be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might ask, why must this witness be allowed to introduce new evidence at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, since the last time a particular witness had testified before this Tribunal, which may have been a number of years previous to their testimony in this case, it's possible that new evidence may have been obtained for which that witness can speak to that's relevant to this case. That is the reason, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this witness would have given a 92 bis statement as recently as possible before giving the testimony and, therefore, would have updated his memory of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, but that presumes that at that time, at the time of the certification process, then that witness is being shown and asked to comment on new evidence that is available at that time. And the Prosecution is simply suggesting that that is simply not always possible. That may not happen, for example, until the witness appears for proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take a slightly -- a slightly nuanced view from that suggested by Mr. Saxon. The reason that the language of "without leave of the Court" has been inserted is because we foresaw, and I mean the Defence - and clearly we have not yet come to a point where our minds are necessarily melding on all issues with regards to how we should view the presentation of evidence and the taking of evidence - but the situation could well occur when an individual, during the certification process, after reading their statement which they are going to be signing for purposes of 92 bis, makes a comment, says, "Listen, there's something in the statement which needs amplification, modification, or correction." In that case, it seems it would be appropriate if such information were to be presented so that the Chamber had an accurate 92 bis statement for that information to be available to the Chamber. Now, that is not necessarily information that would come through the 92 bis process but could be something that occurred thereafter. And in such a situation, where some new information arose, it seemed to be appropriate for the party calling such a witness, calling such evidence, to be in a position to say to the Chamber, "Listen, there's some new information here which directly impacts upon that which is presented in 92 bis, and we'd like the opportunity, with the Chamber's permission, to present such information to the Chamber." So it would be, I believe, in a highly circumscribed situation. That was what our thought was at the time -- I'm sorry. That was what the thought was the Defence had. The reason I'm making a slight distinction here is because Mr. Saxon and I have realised that we heard each other day with regard specifically to paragraph 20, and we thought we understood each other, but it's clear now we were speaking somewhat of a different language with regard to the issues contained in the paragraph. So it's for that reason that I'm making that distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Saxon, would you like to round up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Nothing more to add, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nothing more to add. Thank you so much. And I notice your next input is at paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I begin, I should note, as prefaced by my learned friend, the parties have not reached agreement on final suggestions for the final text of paragraph 20. So, with your leave, I would describe the suggestion to be made by the Prosecution at this time, and I know my colleague will have comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 20, which is entitled "92 ter Witnesses," the Prosecution recommends that the first sentence read: "Rather than filing a motion for each witness who a party intends to call pursuant to Rule 92 ter, that party should provide the other with all relevant materials for each witness three weeks in advance of the testimony of the witness." The following sentence or two sentences is, I believe, where the current lack of full agreement lies. The Prosecution would recommend that the following sentences read: "'All relevant materials' in this context means a notice setting out the prior statements of the witness to be relied upon, with specific passages to be relied upon indicated, relevant passages of prior transcripts, and exhibits from those passages identified from prior statements and prior testimony. A list of remaining documents intended to be used with a witness is to be provided in accordance with paragraph 1 of these guidelines." And the last sentence, which I believe there is agreement on, would read: "The other party should raise any objection 12 days prior to the witness being heard or the Rule 92 ter statement being admitted by the Trial Chamber."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The thrust of the concern here is how do you define "relevant materials" and how do you define "relevant statement"? Our experience has been, with regard to a 92 ter statement, that we receive a consolidated document that contains all of the information upon which the Prosecution relies for purposes of presenting that particular evidence. The Prosecution, as we understand it, suggests the following: If there are two separate statements and one document containing prior testimony, what the Prosecution will do is identify in statement 1, for all the parties and obviously for the Chamber, paragraphs, let's say, 1 through 10, 53, 56, and 92 through 104. In document number 2, the second witness statement, the Prosecution would identify as being part of the 92 ter submission paragraphs 1 through 7, paragraphs - and I'm picking these arbitrarily, obviously - paragraphs 47 through 72 and 95. With regard to the prior testimony of such a witness, the Prosecution would suggest, I assume, that we be looking at page 27946, lines 14 through 19, without having that as a consolidated document, so that we'd all be in a position where we would jumping as between all of these documents at the time when we're dealing with the 92 ter issue. The witness would come to the court, as always, and the Prosecution would say, "Have you read witness statement number 1, and is all of the information contained in witness statement number 1 accurate, and would you so testify if you were to testify to those today?" The witness would say "yes"; and then, of course, we'd go to statement 2 and then we would go the testimony. The difficulty, I think, and I envision here, is that it is probably unworkable; and it also puts us in a position where, when we're trying to make a determination from an objective standpoint of what we object to, we're not looking at it in the context of a consolidated statement. You'll notice that the language here is that of notice, not a statement. The distinction between what notice is and what a statement is, quite frankly, the difference between chalk and cheese. In terms of having a statement, you have a clear document of what the witness would testify to. The difficulties with between 92 already are, I think the Court appreciates, are legion. In as much as it safes time, it is an excellent mechanism to take testimony. In as much as we're going to be dealing with disparate documents that create one particular statement itself, we believe it is going to be a problem. Rather than have that problem, why not create one document that we receive three weeks before or that they receive three weeks before. And to the extent there are any arguments to be made about any specific paragraphs within that document, we'll all be able to deal with it in a very clear, concise, and easy fashion. That's really what the discussion is about. The secondary issue which is the issue of how this paragraph 1 interplays with paragraph 20, because the time provisions of paragraph 1 obviously are five working days before the witness is to testify; whereas, the requirements under paragraph 20 are that any objections to be made with regard to the statement, which of course includes the material upon which the Prosecution or the Defence will rely in presenting a 92 ter statement to the Chamber, requires a three-week period of time. So that there's -- there are two problems with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm pleased to find -- You want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, Your Honour, with your leave. Your Honour, first of all, I believe my colleague slightly misspoke a moment ago. My learned friend referred to the time frame from paragraph 1 as five working days, when actually, I believe, that paragraph refers to two working days. With respect to the merits of what we're discussing, Your Honour, in the Prosecution's experience, what Mr. Guy-Smith is asking the parties to do will create -- will require a great deal of individual, additional work and will actually cause problems rather than -- rather than clarifying the admission of evidence through Rule 92 ter. The attempts to create a so-called consolidated statement will not reduce confusion, Your Honour; it will, in the Prosecution's experience, create confusion. Your Honours, when -- at least with respect to Prosecution witnesses, when Prosecution witnesses who are going to submit their evidence under Rule 92 ter arrive here for proofing, the relevant portion of their statements or the relevant portions of their prior transcripts will be read to them by an interpreter if they are not available in written form in B/C/S. If they are available in B/C/S, then the witness will have a chance to read them to be able to make sure, to be able to testify, that the relevant passages are true and accurate. Mr. Guy-Smith remarked that the key phrase I believe at one point he said is "statement," but the Prosecution submits that the key phrase in this passage in paragraph 20 is the phrase at the beginning, "all relevant materials." And what's necessary here, Your Honours, is that the party that's tendering the evidence under Rule 92 ter provides the other party with sufficient notice of the relevant material that it will rely upon as relevant evidence for this case so that the other party can prepare to test the evidence as laid out. In the Prosecution's experience, the creation of a consolidated statement often leads to additional confusions because we are then creating simply one more additional statement. It becomes, oftentimes, a very large statement and it often then, after it's completed, raises issues of inconsistencies on its own. In the Prosecution's experience, this is a very -- actually, a difficult system to work with, Your Honour, and we would not recommend the Chamber take it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might briefly respond. Having been in two trials, one in which we did not have 92 ter and one in which we did, the last trial, this is a mechanism whereby which we functioned. It seemed to work pretty well, we used it with a fair number of witnesses, and it allowed for a clarity of an understanding of what any 92 ter witness was going to be presenting to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a concern to raise with you gentlemen. I thought that what we are being given here is what the parties have agreed upon and that it's for us to decide whether it's okay, if it is consistent, does it make sense, and then give the guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does look like we have a case within a case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's fine. May I suggest a way forward, because I think time is precious. Can I suggest that you continue talking and get to an agreement, and that when you have agreed, make your recommendations to us and we'll see how we incorporate those and then just give the guidelines, rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- rather than trying to deal with these things and find agreement here in court, instead of trying the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It might have been a good idea to ventilate the issue for a bit of time, but we have been taking time. I do apologise. We'll have further discussion. There have been a couple more agreements which I'll let Mr. Saxon take care of. I should at least flag for the Chamber that with regard to paragraphs 13 and 14, there is no agreement, and the Defence has made some suggestions some time ago with regard to those particular paragraphs, but there has been no agreement. We sent -- we sent tracked changes, as suggested by the senior legal officer, on the 1st of October in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Where the parties are not agreed and the Chamber might think that the matter is relevant, may the Chamber just include that part --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the difficulty is that we have not received a response, so we don't know whether or not we're not agreed at all or whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So the actual factual situation is you have not received a response, not that you're failing to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you find it yourself and then make recommendations to the legal officer and then deal with that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we then move away from the guidelines and hear what the parties have to say on the proofing notes. Who starts, you, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I probably do, because we in the Defence have a constant concern about proofing notes. We've made a suggestion to the Prosecution that they, in some fashion, make verbatim copies of the session in which proofing comes from. We are not asking that those verbatim copies, either through audio or video-recordings, be made available to us in the first instance; but, rather, they be retained so that in the event, unlikely, but in the event that it occurs that a witness, in testifying, when being examined concerning those representations which are made on proofing notes, disagrees with what is contained therein, we have an accurate record of what actually occurred, so that it does not put the Prosecution or, for that matter, the Defence, if such arises, in such a situation where they become either potential witnesses with regard to the credibility, accuracy, or truth of what occurred during the proofing session. It allows all parties, if such occurs, the ability to have the verbatim record of what happened. The Prosecution in that regard has declined this suggestion. It's a suggestion that I made previously in a previous case, and it was declined there also. There were a number of difficulties, which is why we made the suggestion, where witnesses deviated from that which was said in the proofing notes and claimed that that's not what they said. So this seemed to be a mechanism whereby we could address that particular concern. The second issue with regard to proofing notes, and I understand that we've started this case in somewhat of a hurried fashion by virtue of matters that are outside of everybody's control, but the second matter with proofing notes deals with when we get them. Mr. Saxon, with regard to the first witness, has been very kind and has supplied us with three sets of proofing notes; and by three, one was a note where the witness actually changed - and by "change," I don't mean in the negative sense, I mean he read his proofing notes and made corrections - sets of proofing notes. Our concern is we're going to be in a position where at the last minute we're confronted with new evidence that is going to require investigation or the fullness of time for proper preparation. And we understand the difficulties in presenting a case and getting witnesses here and getting witnesses here in a timely fashion such that we can proceed in an orderly way; however, we would like to be able to get those proofing notes sometime other than a day or two right before the witness is to testify. Now, I have no idea what their scheduling system is. I don't know how they do their proofing. Other jurisdictions at this point are disapproving proofing or have certain kinds of disclosure cutoff dates. That's not something that happens here unfortunately, as far as I'm concerned; nonetheless, it's not something that happens here. So we're constantly getting new disclosure as the case develops and, oftentimes, it creates havoc. I'm happy on our side to live with disclosure cutoff dates and delivery dates for the kind of body of information that we are going to be dealing with when a witness testifies. So there are two issues: One is a timing issue and the other is the issue of how to preserve what actually happened during that session. There should be no harm in that whatsoever in terms of the preservation of the proofing session, no harm whatsoever. It's a passive way of obtaining information that would allow all parties, in the event - unlikely, we hope - but in the event that there is a dispute, we have a simply way of resolving it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Judge Bonomy found in the Milutinovic case in December of 2006, witness proofing assists in providing a detailed review of relevant and irrelevant facts in light of the precise charges to be tried and in aiding the process of human recollection and enabling the more accurate, complete, orderly, and efficient presentation of the evidence of witnesses in the trial, and to identify and put the Defence on notice of differences in recollection thereby preventing undue surprise. And as I'm grateful to Mr. Guy-Smith for giving me a compliment at least with respect to my behaviour with the first witness, that is, to date, what we have been trying to do, to provide to the Defence as early as possible any new information, particularly potentially exculpatory information, that arise during a proofing session, and that is what we have done to date. Your Honours, the issue of recording verbatim proofing sessions has been litigated in the Haradinaj case. That Haradinaj Chamber ruled that this was not necessary. It would require the Prosecution to commit additional resources that, quite frankly, it really doesn't have at this point. The Prosecution endeavours and commits itself, both to the Defence and to the Chamber, that our efforts in providing material that arises in proofing will be done to the most accurate degree possible and as expeditiously as possible. Sometimes, we are constrained, for example, by flight times, flight schedules, by abilities to obtain visas by a certain day, which, of course, affects when a witness or witnesses can arrive here and when proofing can begin. But the Prosecution does not see any need at this time for an instruction from the Chamber that proofing sessions be recorded verbatim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just want to mention a concern I have. I don't want to discuss this again. I think it is something that I would urge the parties to agree about outside the court, so that you come to court with something you have agreed on. But for my little knowledge, I'd just like to be educated by you gentlemen. This whole idea of proofing notes being given to the other party is rather new and foreign to me, and I know I saw it for the first time in the last case I was sitting in. And seeing the Defence, in fact, demanding these proofing notes, is this the practice within this Tribunal and is it governed by any Rule that we can look at and say that the Rule says you must give proofing notes? Because I would imagine that if the Prosecution has disclosed the statement of the witness to the Defence, the Defence would not anticipate any other story from that witness other than what they have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, certainly during my ten years here in the Office of the Prosecutor, the provision of proofing notes or, in some cases, supplemental information sheets, has been the standard practice here within this Tribunal. The practice of proofing, to my knowledge, is not regulated anywhere in the Rules. However, we have at least two decisions, two items of jurisprudence - one from the Haradinaj case and one from the Milutinovic case from 12 December 2006 - which describe the reasons for and the appropriateness of this practice. It is, quite frankly, done, proofing notes are provided, again in the interests of being fair to the Defence, so the Defence is not surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then can I, then, urge the parties to agree on how to deal with the question of proofing. Mr. Guy-Smith would like to have verbatim copies. You say you can only give as close to as correct as possible the copy that you're able to give, and then there's also the question of the timing of that. I would like the parties to try and pursue that and save this Court's time from trying to resolve this and come to an agreement right now, and then word it into the guidelines. To me, it seems to be a guideline kind of issue which requires a gentlemanly agreement between the parties. Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm aware of you standing, yes. What do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of timing and based upon what Mr. Saxon has said, I'm sure we can come to an agreement on that. With regard to the issue of resources, I will, once again, make the same offer that I made before, which is I'm more than happy to buy them a recorder - a recorder, a voice recorder - so they have it available. I bought a recorder for the Prosecution the last time which they chose not to use. I'm more than happy to do it again, because they were making a resource claim. So I'm more than happy to buy it for them if they need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't want to get into that. Can you sort that out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I'll be more than happy to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we leave that item on that basis, that you'll continue talking about it, and make a recommendation for purposes of the guidelines. Then the next item was supposed to be protected witness issues. I'm not quite sure who raised it. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, Your Honour. In fact, I'm interested in the position of this Trial Chamber, in view of my prior experience before other Trial Chambers regarding protective measures. I would like to say a few words in principle in public session, and then move into private session. Before one of the Trial Chambers where I worked, every time before the entry of the witness who had been granted protective measures previously, the Trial Chamber considered anew whether there were any reasons to apply them again, and the party who had called the witness had to explain to the Trial Chamber whether they still wanted them applied and to explain why. The other party had to present its arguments as well. Before another Trial Chamber, that had not been the case. Now I would like to move into private session to present further arguments that had been in use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the next matter that's on the list, I think the Chamber will be pleased to note the following, because we can to it quickly: There are a number of exhibits that have yet to be decided that have been the subject of the Prosecution's sixth supplemental motion. Mr. Saxon and I have had a conversation and a number of the exhibits may well come through the next witness, and we have agreed that, with the Court's indulgence, the appropriate way of dealing with those exhibits would have them marked for identification at this time and deal with their admission at a later point in time, because they are still subject to a pending motion that the Defence has not had an opportunity to respond to. That is the beginning and end of that particular matter at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which brings us to the last issue, which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Corrections to Mr. Harmon's opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine, yes. I'm sorry. That's right. That's the next in order. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Harmon asked me to bring something to the Trial Chamber's attention. Yesterday, during Mr. Harmon's opening statement, at pages 13, 29, and 45 of the transcript, Mr. Harmon referred to the "Bosnian Croat army." What Mr. Harmon meant to say and should have said was the "Army of the Serbian Krajina" or "SVK." Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that brings us to the last issue that we had suggested, Your Honour, which is that with regard to the issue of, as I characterised it, and perhaps it's a bit bold, enforcement of prior rulings. The issue here is really very simple; and, once again, I understand that because of some of the things that have happened previously, there has been a scramble on the part of the Prosecution to present witnesses. The witness who we anticipate is the first witness for the Prosecution is a gentleman whose name is Mr. van Lynden. As I understand it, Mr. van Lynden's testimony will revolve around what are termed as "unscheduled incidents." Unscheduled incidents are the subject matter of a decision by this Chamber on the 15th of May, 2007, and specifically the holding was as follows - so I'm assuming it's the law of this case - I'm referring now to the order of paragraph 3 of page 9 of the 15 May 2007 decision: "The Prosecution shall not present evidence in respect of any unscheduled incidents in relation to the Sarajevo counts unless it is able to demonstrate that evidence of certain identified unscheduled incidents in relation to the Sarajevo counts is essential to prove an important aspect of this case. In such case, the Prosecution may file a motion requesting the leave of the Trial Chamber to lead testimony on unscheduled incidents relating to Sarajevo counts at least four weeks in advance of the scheduled testimony, providing reasons for its request. The Defence shall have an opportunity to respond to such a motion." In the body of the decision, in the rationale, the discussion, this Chamber gave an example on paragraph 17 of where it could lead evidence on an unscheduled incident, and that's at the very end, the last or almost the last -- I think it's the second to last sentence, where the Chamber said, and I quote: "It may, however, lead evidence on unscheduled incidents if it can show that such evidence is essential to prove an important aspect of this case." That's what it says in the order, and then there's an example given. "(For example, if an unscheduled incident is necessary to link the accused to the crimes charged)." Now, I am not sure of what is the purpose of Mr. van Lynden's testimony, since his testimony does revolve around unscheduled incidents, and it is clearly -- the presentation is clearly in violation of this particular order. And, once again, I understand the difficulties that the Prosecution has had, and we have not received in any sense whatsoever, whether it be four weeks before or one day before, the basis upon which they are presenting this testimony which deals with the issue of relevance. I thought it would be appropriate to raise this before he testified than to pop up the minute he got on the stand and say, "Objection, relevance, and this is the reason why we're making this objection at this time." Perhaps the Prosecution has a position that they can take in which they can convince the Chamber of the relevance of his testimony, and the timing issue is a different issue whatsoever. But since the order says it, I'm raising it, I read it, I'm trying to follow the Rules. That's what the Chamber said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I understand that a preemptive strike can be a very good means of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I agree with you, but I wasn't meaning it that way. I wasn't trying to -- I was actually trying to deal with it so that I wasn't fiddling with the time being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I still say a preemptive strike may be a good means of defence. May I suggest that we raise that defence at the appropriate time. The Chamber doesn't know, unless maybe the other Judges do, which witness is being called.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let alone what testimony he's going to give. So let's raise the objection and raise the decision of 2007 at the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one little point that I'd like to raise in terms of timing. I know that there are different times of sitting in the different Chambers here, but I was told when I got here, that we sit one hour 15 minutes, take a 30-minute break. So we should have broken at a quarter past. We'll break now and we'll come back at a quarter to 11.00, and it will be one hour 15 minutes, and 30-minute breaks all the time. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution would call Mr. Aernout Baron van Lynden as its first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, is your name Carel Diederic Aernout Baron van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you a citizen of the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever serve in the Dutch Marines?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did, from 1976 until 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you left the Dutch Marines in 1978, what rank did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Second lieutenant and later promoted to first lieutenant in the reserve. This was part of my national service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And did you develop a particular -- a particular specialty during your service in the Dutch Marines?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I was trained as a platoon infantry commander and was trained as a mortary -- mortar platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. van Lynden, after you left the marines in 1978, what profession did you follow?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I became a journalist specialising in war zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what conflicts, what wars, did you cover?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I covered the wars in the Middle East, specifically Lebanon. I lived in Beirut from 1982 to 1986; I covered the Iraq-Iran conflict from 1980 onwards; I covered the fighting in Afghanistan after the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan during the 1980s; and I covered the Gulf War from 1990 to 1991 from Saudi Arabia from the Allied side; and from 1991 onwards I covered the conflict in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during those years as a war correspondent, were you working for newspapers or television or both?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I began as a newspaper correspondent, initially working for the Haagse Courant, the newspaper of The Hague. Later, I became a contract freelancer working for the Washington Post, BBC Radio, and The Observer newspaper in Britain; and in the late 1980s, I switched to working for television, for SkyNews. I worked for them full time, and worked for them until 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, before I forget, you and I speak the same language and we need to be sensitive to the interpreters who are working very hard for us in the booths. So can we make a deal that both of us will try to speak slowly and clearly; and, also, if both of us can try to pause briefly between question and answer, so that the interpreters can have a moment to catch up with us. Mr. van Lynden, what kind of channel or network was SkyNews?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was a 24-hour news channel broadcast by satellite right across Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And -- all right. And you mentioned that you, beginning in 1991, you began to cover the conflict in the former Yugoslavia. In 1991, what part of the conflict did you cover?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: First, Slovenia in June of 1991 until mid-July 1991; then, after a few days' break, I was spent to Belgrade; and I covered the entire conflict between Serbia and Croatia from the Serbian side during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during that time, did you actually go physically to parts of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I did. I went first to Banja and Krajina; later to Eastern and Western Slavonia; and later on, in the autumn, I visited the front, south of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you ever visit a town called Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Regularly. It's somewhere relatively close to Belgrade, which was our base; and we went there from -- in September, October, and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you then make news reports for SkyNews about the events that you observed at the time?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That was the purpose, why I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you explain briefly, how were your news reports sent to SkyNews at the time, and then to other networks. How were they disseminated?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Television news reports are usually sent by satellite. In 1991, we worked -- we actually had an office in Belgrade Television, and the reports were sent from there by satellite to our headquarters in London. What SkyNews in London did with the reports depended on the report itself, but there were certainly moments when Sky gave specifically the pictures to American networks or to one of the two television news agencies in the world, Reuters Television or APTN; usually, Reuters rather than APTN. But many of my reports I am aware of were being sent through to the three American networks, ABC, CBS and NBC; not to CNN because that was considered a competitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you know whether people in Belgrade were able to watch SkyNews reports on their televisions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were. Under an agreement signed between SkyNews and Yugoslav Television in 1989, there was an agreement by my office that they could rebroadcast SkyNews. This was specifically an agreement because they set up something called the third channel in Belgrade; and for, as I remember, 12 hours a day SkyNews was rebroadcast on that channel. Quite apart from that, many Yugoslavs right across Yugoslavia had dishes and could receive SkyNews on those dishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you refer to "dishes," what kind of dishes do you mean?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I mean satellite-receiving dishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did there come a time when the SkyNews broadcasts on that third channel in Belgrade ended?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, I'm not aware or I do not remember the precise moment; but in 1992, it was taken off the third channel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I didn't see the actual document, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to object at this time unless the witness is testifying about something of his own personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the witness can explain what his knowledge is, Your Honour. He hasn't had a chance to provide his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know personally?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We were told by our sources within the Serb government that there was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then I'm going to object on the grounds of -- at this point, on the grounds of hearsay, not because it's mere hearsay, but rather because it's unattributed hearsay. To say "sources from the Serb government" could be any one of a number of different people or individuals or documents. Unattributed hearsay is something that should not be considered by the Chamber, as opposed to, obviously, as we know, hearsay which can be considered. This is a situation in which there is no authorship, there's no way of making a determination of where the information came from, and for that reason I would interpose the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I have one more question, Your Honour, to see if the witness can identify the source or sources?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you withdraw the question that is being objected against for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I wasn't planning on withdrawing the question, Your Honour. I was simply seeing if the witness could identify the source, so it would not be unattributed hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber would have to rule on the objection at this time; so if you don't withdrew it, then the Chamber must rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then I will withdraw that question at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may then ask the question you wanted to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify your source for this information?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Not by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. van Lynden, at some point, did you begin to report about the events in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you briefly, for the Chamber, describe the topography of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Sarajevo is a city that lies by the riverbed of the River Miljacka and runs really from east to west, with hills and mountains overlooking the city to the north and to the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's a long elongated city running along the riverbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, with leave of the Chamber, I would like to show the witness one or two images from the Prosecution's court binder, which I hope that you have. This would be, Your Honours, map number 10 in your court binders. The ERN number is 0424-9162. And, Your Honours, this map -- permission has not been granted to the Prosecution to place this particular image on its Rule 65 -- Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This map is part of a pending motion which Mr. Guy-Smith alluded to. So, with your leave, at this time, I will ask the witness some questions about it, I will ask him to mark some landmarks, and then I will seek at this point only to mark for identification the image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess Mr. Guy-Smith said this morning that that can be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct. That's the agreement that we worked out, with leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The leave of the Court is granted. You may proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're waiting for the image to come up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want the image to come up here. I'm advised that the court officer is having difficulty with this thing. Is it possible to use hard copies until the technician has sorted out the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And does the witness have a hard copy before him at this time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Not at the moment, but we'll give him one, with the assistance of the usher, right now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have extra copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do the Defence have a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, Mr. van Lynden, you should have a satellite image of the city of Sarajevo in front of you. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And for the -- for the orientation of the Judges, first of all, we see the city elongated in this valley floor and we see what appears to be a road running through the centre of the city. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that road is, or was?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The main road through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering, with the usher's assistance, could Mr. van Lynden's map be placed on the ELMO, and then he could view it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see this same map now on the screen in front of you, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, on the monitor to your right, there is a pen attached to it. Maybe with the usher's assistance, there's a marker, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If a pen or a marker could be given to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a pen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But we may need some better pens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I know this may be uncomfortable, but I'm going to ask you to lean over a little bit towards that ELMO, and perhaps if you could draw a line up that main street.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if you could stop right there and just place a number 1 by that green line to indicate that street.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the other end of the street where you stopped the green line --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- do you recall the name of that part of Sarajevo, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was called Stari Grad, the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And could you place a 2, then, besides Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a way we can make Mr. van Lynden's life a little more comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's okay, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll give you a chair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If we can give you a second chair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the microphone could be pushed a little bit more towards Mr. van Lynden's left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can switch between the chairs. That works for me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Saxon, to interrupt you once again. We are now being advised that we can work from e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I switch back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will come back to e-court, Mr. van Lynden, and you will be more comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you could explain what e-court is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You'll see it now on the monitor and you can write on the monitor itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But they will give you a special pen for that. Does Mr. van Lynden have a pen for the monitor? Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm very grateful to Ms. Taseva and her court usher for their patience as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could draw the number 1 there.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The 2 is there by Stari Grad. Do you see an airport on this image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Saxon. I don't know whether this is a disputed issue? It is not a disputed issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify an airport on this image?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you mark the number 3 by the airport?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify a part of Sarajevo known as Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you circle that and put the number 4 by it.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And to the upper left from Dobrinja, are you able to identify that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the neighbourhood of Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you circle that, please, and put the number 5 there.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't know if it's possible or not. Are you able to indicate the general location of the neighbourhood known as Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Only fairly roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But it would be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And, finally --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Do you want me to put a 6 in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Before we move on, going back to that number 1, that long red line --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: -- can you briefly tell us again, what does that red line represent?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's the main road running west to east, or east to west, whichever you wish to see it, through Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. van Lynden, are you familiar with an area known as Zuc?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I went there once in December 1992 with the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify that area on this image?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, this would be pretty rough, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could place a 7 there.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. van Lynden, before we leave this image, I'd like to direct your attention to the higher ground in the upper right-hand corner of the image.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does this image depict all of the high ground in that area?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge. The terrain went further up and -- sorry. It became mountainous, and what was possible from the southern slopes is that one could look right down into Sarajevo and right down various streets in Sarajevo, and this image doesn't completely give that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In May 1992, which forces held that high ground that you see in the upper right-hand corner of the image?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, in May 1992, can you indicate which forces held the remaining high ground above and around the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw a line of the front lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Only if you feel you're able to do that.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is fairly rough because this is a very -- on a very wide scale. The area numbered 6, or the area of Grbavica, was under Serb control. It may have been somewhat larger than this, and their control went wider than that. The precise front lines here I don't know and I didn't know at the time precisely, but it would go here. On this section is the Lukavica barracks, which was held by the Bosnian Serbs throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you draw, please, the number 8 next to that circle.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah. And part of Dobrinja, which I've marked with the number 4, was also in Serb hands. There was a front line running through there. When I first went to Sarajevo in May 1992, the area marked 3, the airport of Sarajevo, was also at that stage in Serb hands. The UN forces had not yet come, as they would later do, to take control of it in July 1992. And an area here, this bit between 4 and 5, or just to the west, was an area called Nedzarici, which was in Serb hands as well. So this was it. Now, here, the precise front lines to -- in the western section at the top right-hand side, I'm not precisely aware of, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Let me see. so this is -- I'm marking the map now as it would have been in -- roughly in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what is it you're marking there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a front line, too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I am right now. But, as I said, Your Honours, this is very rough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. van Lynden, you drew a line from the circle 6 to circle 4. That indicates whose positions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah, that was the Serbs -- the one part within the city of Sarajevo controlled by the Serbs was the area known as Grbavica. The area next to that was Hrasno which, as far as I'm aware, was mostly to the west. The area was called Hrasno and on the other side was Skenderija, and they were in Bosnian hands. Where precisely the front line in the hills was, I can't precisely say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to identify the area known as Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I can mark that with a 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would ask that this image be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This image is marked for identification. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, when you first arrived in Sarajevo in May 1992, eventually did you set up your reporting or your filming base in a particular spot?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. We based ourselves on the top floor of the former military hospital in the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as a television journalist, what was interesting to you or what was important to you about this former military hospital? Why did you set up your equipment there?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was important to us because it gave us -- it was a high building, 12 or 13 storeys high, and it gave us a view from one balcony of the eastern part of the city and the old city of Sarajevo; on the other balcony, at the other side of the building of the newer, western half of the city; and right in front of us was the Bosnian parliament and the actual front lines between the Bosnians and the Serbs. It made it possible for us to film when there was heavy shelling or fighting in or on to the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you first went to that former military hospital and decided to film from the upper floors, did you observe any Bosnian military positions in or around the hospital, Bosnian Muslim positions, Bosniak positions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't, and we actually looked quite carefully.
