The hospital, when we arrived there in May 1992, had already been repeatedly hit and very severely; also not just by machine-gun fire, but also by heavier shell fire. Therefore, we checked very carefully, or as carefully as we could, to see whether it had been used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the extent the witness at this point is speaking in the plural as opposed to the singular, I would object. With regard to his own personal observations, I certainly have no objection. Secondly, to the extent that he is referring to incidents or he's making conclusions with regard to the condition of buildings or conditions of anything else, at this point there's a lack of foundation with regard to his ability to make such observations. It's probably something which is not critical, but I raise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you're saying, Mr. Guy-Smith. Are you saying that the witness is not able to observe with the naked eye the condition of buildings there and tell us how they looked at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm more than -- I'm more than willing to take the position as the Court has suggested, that he can make an observation with the naked eye. To the extent his -- he makes a conclusion as to what he saw, for example, that the buildings were -- had been repeatedly hit, not by machine-gun but also by heavier shell fire, to that extent there is, at this point, no information before this Chamber with regard to his knowledge in that regard. I'm not suggesting he wouldn't be able to say the buildings were destroyed, they were damaged, or something to that extent. But with regard to that particular kind of conclusion, that's where my objection lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your objection is clearer this time. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, then, perhaps if I could lay some foundation, what in your background, knowledge, and experience allowed you to draw some inferences from the damage that you saw?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, I'd spent 13 years in war zones. I lived in Beirut. I know the difference between what a machine-gun, even a heavy machine-gun bullet, can do and what a shell can do to a building. I should point out that the apartment I lived in Beirut itself came under fire. We lost all our outer wall, which was made of glass, on several occasions. I've seen a lot of buildings hit by various forms of artillery - rocket, mortar, and machine-gun fire. I think I can distinguish between the various sorts, without claiming that I can immediately say what kind of millimetre shell would have been used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. And, again, to respond to another objection of my learned friend, when you say that "we" were checking the hospital for indications of Bosnian military positions, who do you mean by "we"?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I should apologise for this use of language, but we were a television crew, three people working together, and, therefore, it's those three people who checked together. Maybe I should have made that clearer in the statement that I made, but I will refer to myself only if the Court prefers that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you and your crew see any indications of -- that Bosnian forces had used that hospital as a military position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer, what do you mean by "Bosnian forces"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I meant the opposing forces to the Bosnian Serb forces, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe if you call them by their name, then you'll be on the wavelength with Mr. van Lynden and with us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you or your colleagues observe any indication that that hospital had been used as a position by the forces that were at that time in opposition to the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We, even on the first night we were there, checked on the roof itself - again, "we" is the two of us went out there, the cameraman and myself - and we looked for, for instance, spent cartridges or boxes that had contained ammunition. We were wary of placing ourselves in a building that was a military target because it was also used for military purposes. We came to the conclusion that it was not. We asked a lot of people as well in Sarajevo and in the hospital whether it had been used by the Bosnian military, and we were told it wasn't. And in all the period thereafter that we were based there, and we were based there for months, we never saw this building or its direct vicinity used by military forces of the Bosnian army or those others opposing the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could please show the witness now on e-court what is 65 ter 9240. It has ERN number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether that image was saved, or did those lines get wiped off?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So it's saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, this image is the next map in your court binder. Just turn the page. You'll see it is a very wide panorama. First, with Ms. Taseva's assistance, if we could zoom in towards the left side in particular on this photograph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, are you able to see the former military hospital on this image?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you take up that magic pen again, and can you put a circle around that military hospital.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And now if we could pan -- well, I've been told, I've been warned by my case manager that I should not try to move this image. So I won't at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, while we have this image here, can you describe what you would be able to see to the right of the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The right of the picture as we see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: So, in this direction, it's towards new Sarajevo, towards the airport, the western side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you draw a number 2 by that arrow, please.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, to the right of the -- to the right of the former military hospital, can you describe what your view was?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Really, the heart of Sarajevo and the Stari Grad, the old city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this image --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we do that, staying with this image for the moment, what could you see, then, in terms of the hills above and around Sarajevo? How was your view there?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From the top floor of the building, when I -- both -- let me just explain. From both 2, the view to the west, and 3, the view to the east, we would be standing on a balcony, a fairly exposed position with some cover, but a fairly exposed position. Right in front, the position looking to the south which was looking over the Bosnian parliament and the front lines, there were no more windows; they'd all been shot out in all the rooms. And, again, this was a very exposed position, only a few hundred metres from the actual front lines. So we had to be very careful going into those rooms. It's not a room that you could just walk into for obvious reasons. But what we could see was the Bosnian parliament, as I said, and then the hills to the south as they rose up, and the district of Grbavica we could see very clearly from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just for the record, the arrow pointing to number 3, that is the view you had to the east of that hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this image could be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The image is admitted into evidence, marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could now -- perhaps if we could move away from this image and call up the unmarked version of this 65 ter number, please, 9240. And if we could move toward the right, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you -- this, if I understand you, this image now depicts an area to the east of that former military hospital?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what part of the city we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Stari Grad, the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you just mark with that pen again the area that you would indicate as Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if this image could be marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The image is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, briefly, if the witness could be shown 65 ter number 9241, this is the next image in your binder, Your Honours, image number 12. It's another panoramic photograph. It's ERN number 0424-9164. And if we could pan towards the right of this image. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, do you see the former military hospital in this image?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around it and the number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What does this image depict for us?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is a picture taken from the south of, let's say, the business heart of Sarajevo, I suppose from the area known as Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And from that military hospital, the former military hospital marked as number 1, to the left we see two large dark-coloured buildings. Do you know what those buildings were?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were called the UNIS towers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you place a circle and the number 2 around those buildings, please?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They are these two buildings. The other high rise is part of the Bosnian parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you place a number 3 next to that high rise part of the Bosnian parliament?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, just to move on, Mr. van Lynden, does this image then show the area more to the west of that former military hospital?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: To the south and to the west, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this image could be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The image is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P4, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, how did you broadcast your reports from Sarajevo at that time, in late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In a complicated manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And could you try to explain that in summary form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And simpler terms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to keep it simple, Your Honours. At the time, SkyNews had sent its own dish with engineers, satellite dish, into Bosnia, but the engineers and the dish were in Pale, which was the headquarters of the Bosnian Serbs, together with the editing equipment and the picture editor of the stories. What was required from us was that on a daily basis my cameraman, George Davies, and myself would have to drive across the front lines of Sarajevo and into the area of Ilidza where we would encounter our producer, hand over the tapes. Then he would drive through Ilidza, across Sarajevo airport, past Lukavica, around to Pale. There the story would be edited and then fed by satellite to London. We would then have to cross the lines again into Sarajevo. There is a basic rule for war correspondents: Don't cross lines. In Sarajevo, at that stage, we had to do it on a daily basis and it was always dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, how about after May, during the summer of 1992, how did you broadcast your reports?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In May and June, what I've just explained was how we did it. We returned towards the end of June. At this stage, the UN had moved into the airport, and we then brought with us into Sarajevo the satellite dish that I had earlier described as being in Pale, and then we no longer had to cross lines to feed our stories to London, to send our stories to London.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, as a reporter, for you and your team, what benefits did this arrangement give you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The obvious one of not having to cross lines and be shot at every time we had to get a story out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And apart from that?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Having your own satellite dish, if you work for television, meant that we could do live reports; that is to say, the correspondent standing in front of the camera answering questions asked in realtime by a presenter in studio. This was something we had not been able to do before and we were then able to do in -- towards the end of June and July and August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall where in Sarajevo you positioned that SkyNews satellite dish?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It didn't actually belong to SkyNews. It was hired, it was rented for a period, and we put it into part of the Kosevo hospital duplex, into a building that still under construction that had not been finished, and where it was relatively safe and protected on three sides by concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, this is a different hospital from the former military hospital that we've discussed previously?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Absolutely. The Kosevo hospital is the academic, the teaching hospital of Sarajevo. The former military hospital, as its name implied, was the military hospital and has since changed its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the SkyNews -- I shouldn't use that term. Did this rented satellite dish remain in the Kosevo hospital throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, it did not. It was moved out of Sarajevo when I was not there, either at the end of August or at the beginning of September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And so, after that, by the beginning of September, then, how did you broadcast your reports?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In September, I worked out of Pale, the Bosnian Serb headquarters, and there we were able to use Serb television facilities to send our stories from Pale to Belgrade Television, and from there they were satellited on to London. In October, November, and December, when I was in Sarajevo, or at least at the end of October 1992 until December 1992 I was in Sarajevo, and then we sent the stories through the satellite dish brought into Sarajevo by the European Broadcasting Union and set up at TV Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. van Lynden, what was the subject of your very first SkyNews report from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: As I recall, it was a story simply of what it looked like on the streets of Sarajevo and of how people, the civilians, had to run when they were crossing streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did these people have to run when they were crossing streets?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because they were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think, at this point, we are beginning to approach what I was discussing previously. This question calls for information which is outside of the indictment period and may well run afoul of the Court's decision of 15 May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with leave of the Chamber, I can present, describe the relevance of this information to the events of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My concern, Mr. Saxon, is that is this the time to demonstrate the relevance or should it have been demonstrated at the time the motion was made; and if it wasn't, what's the good cause, what's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the good cause was simply, in the Prosecution's haste to prepare for this witness and get this witness here, the Prosecution omitted attending to such a motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate the dilemma the Prosecution may have had in terms of getting witnesses here. This was a subject that we dealt with sometime before we began this trial. The Prosecution's choice of witnesses was entirely up to them. I actually even made a suggestion of a witness who they had available that could have taken care of some of their difficulties. That suggestion was rejected for whatever reason. Be that as it may, the fact of the matter is that as this particular witness sits here now and the information that the Prosecution is attempting to elicit from him, we have not had an opportunity to respond to any objections we may have to the asserted basis of relevance, which puts us in an uncomfortable position of having to either object to each and every question as they are propounded and answered or puts us in a position of having some submission from the Prosecution with regard to the relevance and allowing us some period of time to consider what their position is and respond in an intelligent fashion so that the Chamber has the benefit of our opinion based upon the preexisting order. Now, I understand that we are clearly not in a four-week situation just because of the manner in which we find ourselves; however, we have no information whatsoever with regard to the issue of relevance. I'd like to have that information so that I could respond. We may take the position that we don't disagree and it is relevant. We may well have objections to certain aspects of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to Mr. Saxon demonstrating the relevance right now, which is what he's asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have an objection to him demonstrating the relevance in the presence of the witness. In the absence of the witness, I have no problem to him demonstrating the relevance. How we will respond to that and whether or not we will have the fullness of time to respond to that is another issue. I don't know whether, once he does that, whether or not I will be called upon to immediately respond to the issue of whether or not it's relevant or not. I may request a bit of time. I understand, once again, that it's at the beginning of the trial and we're kind of pressed because of, as I said earlier, matters that are outside of anybody's control. But the Prosecution chose to call this particular witness at this time, and I think at some level we at least need the ability to respond to it in some intelligent fashion. I'm not asking for a four -- I'm clearly not asking for a four-week period, but I may need some period of time. Then, again, he may convince me. I just don't know. But outside of the presence of the witness, I would prefer because that's what would have normally happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm prepared to make that submission, Your Honour, outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. van Lynden, will you please excuse us for some time? We'll call you when it's completed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Indeed, before Mr. Saxon starts, the reason that I flagged this issue a little bit earlier was an attempt to flag time, so people could at least have some advanced warning of what the issue may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance of this witness' evidence pertaining to the events pre-indictment period in 1992, the first half of 1993, exists on several levels. First of all, the accused is charged with criminal responsibility for crimes against humanity that occurred in the city of Sarajevo, and the evidence from 1992 that this witness could provide is relevant to show the widespread and systematic nature of the attacks on civilians and civilian areas in the city of Sarajevo beginning in 1992 and continuing through 1995. Secondly, Your Honour, the relevance of this evidence is more personal, if I can put it that way, directly personal to this accused. This evidence will be relevant to the charges against Mr. Perisic pursuant to Article 7.1 of the Statute, to show that Mr. Perisic was aware of the substantial likelihood that the participation in the provision of weapons, ammunition, and other material to the Army of Republika Srpska would have a substantial contribution to the commission of crimes in Sarajevo, as described in schedule A of the revised second amended indictment. So this evidence from 1992 is relevant to the amount of information and notice that Mr. Perisic received vis-a-vis the mens rea element of aiding and abetting. Thirdly, Your Honour, the evidence from 1992 is relevant to the allegations in the revised second amended indictment that pursuant to Article 7.3 of the Statute, Mr. Perisic bears criminal responsibility for the crimes that occurred in Sarajevo and listed in schedule A. This evidence is relevant to demonstrate that, given the information available to Mr. Perisic about the events occurring in Sarajevo, that Mr. Perisic knew or had reason to know that his subordinates in the Army of Republika Srpska were about to commit or had committed these crimes. And this is a matter in dispute, Your Honour. The Defence, in their pre-trial brief, paragraph 135(u), state that the Defence contest the Prosecution assertion that Mr. Perisic was fully informed about the events, alleged, including violations of international law that had occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, I would direct you to jurisprudence from the Boskoski and Tarculovski case, case number IT-04-82-T, oral decision, presiding Judge Parker, on the 2nd of July, 2007, page 2921 of the transcript, where the Trial Chamber held that: "Publication of information about acts committed by the subordinates of a superior accused during the pre-indictment period can give the superior, 1, notice of the possibility and prospect of misconduct by his subordinates, and, 2, should subsequent allegations of misconduct occur during the indictment period, give the superior additional reason to act on information about the crimes that occurred." So, on these three different levels, Your Honour - widespread and systematic, mens rea of Article 7.1 responsibility, the mens rea of Article 7.3 responsibility - the evidence of this witness from 1992, in the Prosecution's submission, is highly relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that the wisdom of the Court's previous ruling becomes self-evident in terms of giving the Defence an opportunity to respond. It would not be responsible at all for me to respond to the arguments just made by Mr. Saxon concerning this very important issue in haste, and I will need some time to respond to those arguments, as they have been set forth. This is not a situation in which I feel comfortable at all rapidly reposting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. Guy-Smith, is that this Trial Chamber has to make a ruling on this objection and this witness must carry on with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, that's the reason why I raised the issue before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The problem is at this point that there -- from what I understand Mr. Saxon's argument to be, at first blush, it, in fact, requires a re-examination of this Chamber's previous order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understand that previous order, it says that the Prosecution or a party is not allowed to cover testimony outside the indictment period unless it can demonstrate the relevance of that testimony to the act and conduct of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in total agreement with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then it has a secondary part which is, and if such a situation arises where the Prosecution chooses to do so, they have to give advance notice so that the Defence can respond, and that's the problem here. Not that if they make a showing of relevance, that they're entitled, obviously, after the Chamber's determination, to adduce the evidence - I'm in total agreement with that - but, rather, that we need a chance to respond. I've seen what Mr. Saxon has said. Perhaps it was not the best thing to tell him beforehand of what my concern was; but because I was concerned about breaking up the testimony of the witness, I figured it would be better to raise it beforehand, as soon as I realised that we were -- what kind of evidence we were dealing with and that this would be the first witness called, than to raise it at a later point in time. So I find myself -- I find myself in a bit of a dilemma. I understand the Court's concern, I understand what the Court wishes to do, but I don't believe that I would be doing justice to Mr. Perisic at this point if I shot from the hip on this particular issue. What I would ask for, if that is not unreasonable, is I would ask for some very short period of time in order to respond; "short period of time" meaning at least a day, at least a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you asking for an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am. I think that's the most probably what I am doing. I think it's the most prudent thing to do and that's what I'm doing, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you're still on your feet, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm trying to figure out whether there is an interim solution, which is perhaps to the extent there is other evidence to be led through this witness which does not cause the particular area of concern, we could at least proceed with that evidence so that we could meaningfully use the Court's time. Then we would only have this one discrete area which now has been articulated by the Prosecution. And if the Chamber is so inclined, we could have some time to respond. I'm trying to figure out how to use the time. It may be another way of grabbing some more time. I don't know if that works for Mr. Saxon or not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in all frankness, the amount of evidence that would not be touched by this issue would really only be a small fraction of the remaining evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, the view of the Chamber is that this is really a very simple issue. The question of whether or not there was widespread attack on civilian population and whether the accused had notice of it is part and parcel of proving the case, where you've got to prove the element of whether the person had notice or didn't have notice. It is a little difficult for the Trial Chamber to fathom how much of this day you would need to be able to respond to this explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm in the habit of not fighting with the Chamber, and when a Chamber makes the kind of pronouncement that you've just made, I am trying to figure out a way of retreating ever so slightly yet still maintaining the position that I have with concern for my client. In that regard, what may well be a way of attending to the immediate issue is for me to note the objection on the record, for Mr. Saxon to proceed with his examination with an understanding that that aspect of the evidence, assuming that I have an argument against what he said, once I've had a chance to reflect during the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are actually at break time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- during the break, and then if I have a further objection, I'll note the objection. Then if the Chamber feels it appropriate to strike the testimony at a later point in time, they may; and if you feel it's appropriate to keep the testimony and consider it, you'll give it whatever weight you deem appropriate. I'm trying to come up with a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. It is, indeed, the proper time for the break. The Chamber will refrain from making a ruling to allow you to be thinking about the matter during the break, and when we come back at half past 12.00, we will take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Court adjourned. We'll come back at half past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I've had an opportunity to reflect. I have but a few comments and then I'll leave it in your capable hands. Looking at the indictment, specifically paragraph 40, which identifies a period for aiding and abetting between 1993 August and November 1995, specifically with regard to Sarajevo, and addressing paragraph 45 in which the Prosecution has alleged, A, the crimes involved numerous individual criminal acts that were perpetrated over an extended period of time in the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and, B, that crimes received widespread attention from the media, inter-governmental organisations, international negotiators, and non-governmental organisations, many of which base their reports on the first-hand accounts of the crimes, which refers back to the period that I'm referring to, between August of 1993 and November of 1995, and taking into account this Chamber's pronouncement in the decision that I raised before, paragraph 17, the Trial Chamber, and I quote: "However, finds that the scheduled incidents, having regard to all the relevant circumstances, including the crimes charged in the amended indictment, their classification, nature, the places where they are alleged to have been committed, their scale and victims of the crimes are reasonably sufficient -- are reasonably and sufficiently representative of the crimes charged." Then the Chamber goes on into the rationale that I've discussed beforehand. I don't believe that the Prosecution is contending that between August of 1993 and November of 1995 that there was no media attention in Sarajevo upon which their need, as the Court has appointed out appropriately, to prove notice would not be based. And if notice, which is, as I understood you right before the break, one of your concerns - and I understand why it is and I don't disagree that that is one of the things that they must prove - if notice is to be proved, then it should be proved during the indictment period considering that the Chamber already has dealt with the issues as to their extent and their scale. Apart from that, and I raise it because - I don't know if we'll ever get in the situation again; I hope that we don't - we have been placed in not necessarily an untenable position but certainly an unfortunate one procedurally by virtue of the Prosecution's failure to follow an order, an order which they actually acknowledged in a filing sometime after this Court's decision. That was, I believe, when they filed one of the requests for revised 65 ter list. It is an awkward position to be in for the Defence and it creates a difficulty for us; however, I will leave my remarks at that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. I don't know whether you anything have to say, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Let me suggest a way forward here because I think time is of the essence; namely, that we will hear the witness, and if at any other stage the Defence feels that the testimony has to be expunged maybe for further reasons that you may have, then that part of the testimony will be expunged at that time. But I think since the witness is here, let's hear what he's got to say, and get done with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome. You may call the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, let me just apologise on behalf of the Trial Chamber for getting you out of the court while you were testifying. It's one of those procedural things that we try to avoid. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before you left the courtroom, Mr. van Lynden, I believe I asked you, what was the subject of the first SkyNews report that you did in Sarajevo. Can you tell us what that was, please?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. It was about what life on the streets of Sarajevo looked like and it included shots of people running across streets, and they were running across streets because they were afraid that they would be shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to "people running across streets," are you referring to soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: These were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you refer to "people running across streets because they were afraid that they would be shot at," these civilians, if you know, which force or forces were the source of this shooting that induced this fear?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This was shooting that was coming from the southern hills overlooking Sarajevo and was done by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why did you decide to do a report about -- or part of your report about the persons running across the streets?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because it was rather different to the way that most of us go about our business as civilians in the cities in which we live. It marked Sarajevo as being a different city to others. I should add that I lived in Beirut during four years of war there, a city divided by what was called the green line; and while there were areas close to that green line that were dangerous for anyone venturing there, it was not as if people in Beirut couldn't get on with their daily lives in most of the rest of the city. They often could. In Sarajevo, that was markedly different because of the terrain of the city, because it was this elongated city sitting in the valley bed, and that those who were firing on the city help positions higher and could literally look down the streets of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I'd like to show a portion of video material to Mr. van Lynden. This video material was not shot by Mr. van Lynden or his SkyNews team. It was taken by a resident of Sarajevo by the name of Zoran Lisic during September or October of 1992. But Mr. van Lynden can speak to this video clip so I'd like to show it, and then ask him some questions about it. So we will begin this clip, and then we will -- this is from 65 ter number 3062 from 9 minutes to 9 minutes and 20 seconds, and we will begin and then stop at 9 minutes 04.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, again, just to be clear, when you were present in Sarajevo in 1992, did you personally observe persons running across intersections, such as the image we have at 9:05.2 on the screen in front of us?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we go forward, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go back, though, to the last scene, please. I didn't want to take that away, the last image that we had at 9:20. Okay. We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, we see parked across that street a large blue truck. This is at 9:21 of the -- this video clip. It seems to have some material inside it. Did you observe such large trucks parked in intersections in 1992 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: There were trucks there with containers placed at intersections, one on top of the other. There were tarpaulins that were hung down streets. So, yes, the answer is yes, and I imagine this one was -- and it looked like it was filled with earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the purpose, if you know, of placing these large trucks or containers across streets or intersections?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: To allow the civilians walking on foot, or actually those driving by car, to cross those intersections more safely and to take them away from the sight of those in the hills above the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often did you observe such scenes of people running in Sarajevo during your time there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: On a daily basis, every single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if I can ask, how do these scenes of people running depicted in this video clip compare to the scenes that you reported on in your first report of SkyNews?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were fairly similar, the only difference being that in that first report, we also had an elderly man, a stooped elderly figure, as I remember, with a walking stick trying to go as quickly as he could, but he couldn't actually run.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, did you ever personally observe civilians who had been struck by gunfire from Bosnian Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I never actually saw the it, the actual moment of impact that they were hit, but we saw at various times people who had been wounded or killed by such gunfire lying on the streets or lying on the pavements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, again, when you refer to "people," are you referring to civilians or military personnel?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would seek to tender this video clip from 9:00 to 9:21, from 3062. The ERN number, do we have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. As I understood this, this was not a video clip that was broadcast, but rather was a video clip upon which the witness was indicating that it was representative of some other -- some of the things that he saw. To the extent that it is, one, an unscheduled incident, two, outside of the indictment period, and, three, would not serve the ostensible period of notice, I would object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point is, regarding notice, the witness testified that he did, he produced a report for SkyNews quite similar to this report, and that is why this video clip is relevant to notice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if that be the case, then let's produce that. let's produce that video with regard to the reason in which the Prosecution is seeking to introduce this particular evidence. Now we're one step removed in regard to an unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously, the best evidence rule applies in this courtroom and in this Tribunal, and the Prosecution has not been able to locate Mr. van Lynden's first report containing footage similar to the footage you have just seen. In the Prosecution's submission, this, then, is the best evidence that we have available.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, from an evidentiary standpoint, there are two distinct issues here now. This is not the best evidence of a broadcast, which is what we are referring to here. This gentleman has a video clip which was broadcast. This particular video clip, apart from authentic ethnicity issues, and when it was taken which is at this point kind of rough - we have a period of months - and a series of other issues have not been addressed. I, quite frankly, think that Mr. Saxon is using the best evidence rule in kind of a curious way. He is -- actually, what he's doing is he's substituting a kind of evidence for the reality of a situation that he's attempting to portray through this witness which is broadcast information, which is the important point I'm dealing with, broadcast information, not a condition that may have existed at a particular time but rather that that information served as, as he told us in the beginning for purpose of relevance, as a notice, and therein lies the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. We are with your colleague, Mr. Saxon. The problem is that if this particular video was not broadcast, how does it serve as notice to the accused? Is it possible for you to keep searching for the video that was taken by Mr. van Lynden and tender it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Certainly, it is possible, Your Honour, and we will endeavour to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you could. For that reason, then, this video will not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honours. At this time, I would like to show the witness a series of video footage that were produced by this witness and his crew in Sarajevo and broadcast on SkyNews. Just for the record, the series of video clips that you'll see soon, Your Honours, all were previously admitted in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic as part of Exhibit D192 and in the Galic trial as part of Exhibit P/540.5.1. One technical matter, Your Honour, before we show the first clip. The clips have the B/C/S translation -- transcript, I should say, visible underneath the video footage itself so that the accused can follow along what is being said. Everyone else, of course, can listen to the English. The question is whether the Chamber prefers that our colleagues in the B/C/S interpretation booth also read that B/C/S transcript as the video is playing so that will become part of the record of this trial as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't take the record in B/C/S, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I meant in an audio sense, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In an audio sense. Well, to the extent possible, I think if the interpreters in the B/C/S can interpret that, I'm not quite sure whether they are not going to be disturbing Mr. Perisic while he's trying to read himself what is on the screen, and then he hears people talking over his head and disturbing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But whichever way is convenient. I'm not sure whether the Defence has any comment to make on the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Mr. Perisic will find it easier to follow if he reads the text from the screen; and if there accidentally occurs a discrepancy, that might cause a confusion. So I really don't think the interpreters need to read the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then the B/C/S interpreters don't need to read. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this video clip, a SkyNews broadcast, was filmed on the night of the 4th/5th of June, 1992. This is Prosecution 65 ter number 4347. The entire length of this video footage is 3 minutes, 35 seconds; however, we will only show 1 minute and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, right at the very beginning of this clip, at 00:00:4, can you explain what you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yeah. This -- this would have been put on in London at SkyNews. Every story that is run in a news broadcast has a slug, has a name. The programme is the 2100 programme. This would have been British summertime, the day was a Friday, and then the date that it was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So, when you say the date of the broadcast, what, then, should we infer about the day or date when the footage was actually taken?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Because, as I have explained to the Court, the procedure of getting my footage back to London was a complicated one at this stage, the footage that you are about to see was filmed the previous day or on the morning of the 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can begin this clip, please, and stop at 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Dusk in Sarajevo, amongst the city's ancient minarets, the rockets fall, heralding another night of heavy shelling."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, if you can tell us, we see some smaller lights going that are going across the screen here. Are you able to tell us what kind of fire we're seeing?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What we're seeing here is machine-gun fire, probably of various different calibres, and, quite possibly, including 20 and 30-millimetre anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: For the record, whose voice do we hear on this clip?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This is my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where was this fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This fire was coming from, yeah, the Bosnian Serb-held positions south -- on the southern side of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On this evening, did you see any outgoing fire from within Sarajevo towards the positions of the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From within Sarajevo, not. There was fighting on the front lines as well; and there, there would have been outgoing fire. But I did not see from any position within the city proper any outgoing fire, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's keep going, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "For the next six hours, there is no letup. Eerily let up by flares, the city is hit from every side by practically every imaginable projectile. Long lines of heavy machine-gun fire gliding across the roofs, exploding against their targets."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stopping here at 1 minute, 14 seconds, we're seeing this fire coming into the city of Sarajevo at night. If you can tell us, based on your experience and knowledge, machine-gun fire, rocket fire, is it, at night, more accurate during the day, less accurate, or it doesn't make any difference?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: For any observer observing the fire and, therefore, then telling the battery commander, for instance, within an artillery unit, I would say that it is more difficult. My experience tells me it's more difficult, and those who are professionals in that work have told me that it is more difficult to direct that fire accurately at night than it is during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Heavy shells slamming into buildings, within seconds engulfing them in claims. A mass of crazy sparks lighting the brow of one hill from a quite-fire folly of mortar bombs. This is a scene of wholesale devastation of a city being obliterated while the world watches but does nothing."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that you we saw on the screen a couple seconds ago at around 1:45, 1:50?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You commented about -- made comments about wholesale devastation and a city being obliterated. Why did you believe that Sarajevo was being obliterated?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: What we were witnessing - and this was for hours and this is only a very small part of what was filmed - was a variety of shells, mortar bombs, and, as I've already mentioned, different calibre machine-guns or anti-aircraft fire, hitting the city but hitting it all over the place. It wasn't that it was just one particular spot that was being targeted, but these various projectiles were hitting right across the city. It was of a nature that was very heavy, indeed, and we felt that the whole city was being targeted. That was our impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the night this footage was made, did you observe any concentrated fire directed at a single target?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, not really. There were those moments, for instance, where what I describe as mortar bombs on the brow of one hill, when a number of projectiles did hit one particular spot, or at least appeared to from the distance we were at and looking and filming it. But most of it was all over the place and it seemed very random.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, are you familiar with how professional armies use artillery?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I am, I think. I'm not an artillery -- I was not an artillery officer, but I was trained in the use of mortars; and during the Gulf War, I spent quite a lot of time with both British and American artillery units. It was explained then by the officers commanding those units precisely how such an artillery battery would function and what the purpose of it was. What we witnessed in early June 1992 in Sarajevo was, apart from the bombardment of the Marsal Tito barracks, completely different from what I had been told and what I'd seen earlier, which was that one particular target would be taken and come under sustained fire. There would be one, two, or three rounds fired initially so that an observer could say to the battery commander that the target had been actually hit, and then there would be sustained artillery fire on that target, with usually the purpose of the military being that such an artillery barrage would be followed up by some kind of move by infantry or armoured infantry or tanks into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, what effect did this kind of shelling or machine-gun fire have on the inhabitants of Sarajevo? What effect could you observe?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Fear. People lived as much as they could in the basements of their apartments or in bomb shelters, and people were made fearful because they became aware that wherever they were -- may be living in the city, they could be hit by either an artillery shell or a mortar bomb or heavy machine-gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would seek to tender into evidence this video footage along with the attached transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video footage is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P5, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can leave this video footage for a moment, I would like to show the witness what is Prosecution 65 ter number 4347.01, which was footage shot on the night of the 5th and 6th of June, 1992, and we will stop at 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marsal Tito barracks, it becomes the night's prime target. The shells land long."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We have lost sound. Can we try it again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Just hours after the evacuation of the troops from the Marsal Tito barracks, it becomes the night's prime target. The shells land long."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously, we have a technical problem. Let's stop here at 23 seconds, point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can explain to us, Mr. van Lynden, what were the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo, and where was it located?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Marsal Tito barracks were the main barracks of the JNA, the Yugoslav Army, inside Sarajevo, a large complex predating the communist regime in Yugoslavia and located just to the west of the former military hospital, from which this is being filmed. In the current picture, you can see part of the Marsal Tito barracks in the bottom right-hand corner of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before this evening, the night of the 5th and 6th, who held control over the JNA barracks, before that evening, the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was still in the hands of the JNA until an agreement was reached that day for the evacuation of those troops out of the barracks and out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And before we do, again, just for the record, whose voice do we hear on this video clip?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Around Sarajevo's railway yard, but inside the vast army complex, those still looking for loot get the message and run. Not long after the gunners in the hills above the Bosnian capital find their range. The barracks explodes in flames. The barracks form the principal target, yet no district escapes. Through the dark, the rockets streak down, for a moment illuminating Sarajevo's ancient centre, before reducing it to further rubble. They come in ones, in twos, in threes, and it sounds as if the city's crying. At 3.00 in the morning, the barracks are again bearing the full weight of attention ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We're stopping now at 1 minute and 27 seconds, and we see here the Marsal Tito barracks on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where was this shelling coming from, whose forces, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the kind of and the character of the shelling of the Marsal Tito barracks on the night of the 5th to the 6th of June, 1992, consistent with the other shelling of Sarajevo that you had observed by that time, or not?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, this was different. This was clearly sustained fire on one target. We were aware that the JNA, in withdrawing from the barracks, had not been able to take all its equipment with them; and this was clearly, in our analysis, an attempt on the part of the Bosnian Serbs to see to it that that equipment did not fall into the hands of their opponents. It was sustained shelling of that target that night and the night that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please, and we'll stop at 1 minute, 37 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: " ... of this vast but now deserted military complex aflame. With light the people rarely come out to inspect the damage, recover what ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, why did you film this particular scene? This is at 1:37.4. We see people carrying what appears to be a bed out of a store or out of a store area.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Every day that we were there this in period, the heavy shelling took place in the late afternoon and during the nighttime hours; and during the day, we would drive around town to see how bad the damage was, to try and find out, of course, also casualty figures, not only at the hospital in which we were staying where it was relatively easy to figure out, but also the Kosevo hospital and other hospitals, and to see the damage and to see how people reacted to that. This was a scene we had come across of a store where there had clearly been damaged because of the shelling, and people were taking things out of the store because the store was clearly no longer tenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we move forward now to what will be 2 minutes and 18 seconds of this video. Start from there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: GANIC: "...they're destroying the city and they're buying time by signing the agreements. But we, you know, we did our best, we cooperate with UN, we belong to that family, and we hope the Security Council will act quickly." THE REPORTER: "So does the small UN contingent here ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That last scene we saw a gentleman wearing a tie speaking from about 2 minutes, 25 seconds, to 2 minutes and 30 seconds. Who was that man speaking?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was Ejub Ganic, the vice-president of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when he referred to "they," they were destroying the city or their buying time, who is the "they" that he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would seek to admit this footage into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, is it the Prosecution's intent to introduce at this point int time only those portions that were shown to the witness or the entire -- I'm seeing nodding, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Only those portions that were shown to the witness and are now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I'm clear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then. The video clip, 65 ter 4347.01, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. [The Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Registrar says that from this video clip, two portions were shown and the in-between portion was not shown. Do you want two numbers or one number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Two numbers, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Two numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And I should also should have said, Your Honour, that these video portions should have -- also be admitted -- well, along with these video portions, the transcripts of this video is 65 ter number 4348, in English and B/C/S. If those could be admitted as well, Your Honour, to form part of the record, the transcripts that you saw going across the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly have no objection to that methodology. I rose only for purposes of indicating to the Chamber that rather than standing up with regard to each video clip that we are shown which is of an unscheduled incident, we do have an continuing objection based on the arguments made previously. I just figured I'd do it one time as opposed to jumping up for each video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then the video clip, together with the transcripts that go with it, will be admitted into evidence. I'm not quite sure, but I guess the video clip with its own transcript will get one exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video clips shown will be Exhibit P6 and Exhibit P7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, I'd like to show you now a SkyNews broadcast and the -- you'll see this is 65 ter 4347.02.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you go to the beginning, please, and stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You'll see it's -- on the SkyNews clock, it says "7 June 1992." So would it be fair to say that the footage was then produced on the 6th of June?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we begin, and then we'll stop at 35 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "It was the symbol of modern Sarajevo, now of its destruction. Flames tear across the floors and up into the higher storeys, showering debris onto the streets of the heart of the Bosnian captain, the disintegration of one of the city's UNIS towers reflected in the broken windows ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: These UNIS towers, you had marked them on a map previously and you refer to them as the symbol of modern Sarajevo. What were they used for at that time?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: They were office buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And where was the fire hitting the UNIS tower that was on fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Again, from the Bosnian Serbs, southern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was that your voice that we heard?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you able to observe the kind or kinds of munitions that struck the UNIS tower that evening?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The building was already on fire when we arrived at the former military hospital, and we had been in another part of Sarajevo during the day. As I recall, we came somewhere in the latish afternoon, 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon, and the building was already on fire. So we did not witness the beginning of the fire in the UNIS towers. What we witnessed and filmed after that was specifically machine-gun fire being directed at the sort of lower part of the building. But as far as I recall, no large shell or any large projectile hit the UNIS towers after we had arrived. It simply burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on that day, the 6th of June, did you see any outgoing fire from the UNIS towers or the area around the towers, fire directed towards the positions held by the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please, until 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "... of its twin. Three-hundred metres on across the road, the parliament of this newly independent state is also struck."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, we've stopped at 56.1, but at 55 we saw a flash and buildings were illuminated at that time. What were those illuminated buildings?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: That was the parliament building in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the parliament building composed of one building or two?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Well, there's a lower building and then there's a tower block right next to it, and my understanding is that's all part of the same -- that's all part of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's fine. Now we have a better view. We see -- can you describe what we're seeing here at 1 minute, 2 seconds, Mr. van Lynden?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the right-hand side of the screen is the tall office block of the parliamentary office complex, and then on the lower left-hand side is the lower building that is also part of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this bright light was caused by what, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Either a shell or a rocket --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: -- hitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue, please, and stop at 1 minutes and 17 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "It doesn't burn, but the nearby Marsal Tito barracks do. Since its evacuation two days early, it's being systematically destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We just saw, the last few seconds, we see it now on the screen, it appears to be footage shot in daylight. So can you explain, was the footage of the Marsal Tito barracks taken at the same time as the shelling of the UNIS tower and the parliament?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I mean we were continuously filming that late afternoon, evening, and night, but I think the sequence of events, as put together by the picture editor, was that he began with the first shots that the cameraman, George Davis, took of the UNIS towers burning; and then he put in two shots of the parliament being hit before moving on to the Marsal Tito barracks. That has to do with the way that I had, of course, scripted the story. It looks from these pictures as if we're slightly going from daytime to nighttime and back to daytime again. That's partly due to my script and it's also partly due to the fact that I did not have direct control over the editing as I was not in the same place as the editor who was at that time in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we keep going as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: THE REPORTER: "Every night in Sarajevo you think it can't get worse, but it does making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to this city which is enfolded in war. Less than 24 hours earlier, the Serb commanders had put their signatures on yet another agreement, affirming a truce never adhered to and their readiness to reopen the airport. Now the Serb gunners in the hills show where their true commitment lies. Under a sickle moon, the city rocks to the explosions, lit up by fire and the mass of glowing sparks adrift across its roofs. With daylight we find the intensive care wards of the city central hospitals packed with amputees in pain. Some will live, but the doctors are resigned to this girl's death. Not far from where she lies do others that have gone before; a place of haphazard death, some covered, some not, where maggots crawl the floors. A little house of Bosnian horror. "Aernout van Lynden, SkyNews, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where did you shoo this last footage where we see a number of dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: This in the morgue of the Kosevo hospital, the main academic hospital in Sarajevo, And the earlier picture of those who were injured was also shot at the Kosevo hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in the last seconds of this footage from 2:40 to 2:45, we saw a young boy -- we saw someone who appeared to be a boy. Do you know how old this person was, this body?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: I believe he was eight or nine years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know how he died?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: From shrapnel wounds, we were told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He was asked if he knew. He's relying on hearsay. I don't know if it's attributed or unattributed hearsay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I was in the morgue, I saw the boy, and I asked the man looking after the morgue how he had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. Does the man have a name? Once again, it's unattributed hearsay. I mean, this is a problem, and I -- I mean, the conclusions made about how he died is distinct from the issue of whether or not he was dead, to which I have no objection. This also calls for -- is a conclusion which is based upon a different form of expertise and certainly not one that this gentleman has; and if he has information which is given to him by somebody who does, then, of course, I take a different position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has testified from whom, without giving a particular name, he received this information about the death of this young man. Yes, that is hearsay. Having said that, Your Honour, hearsay evidence is admitted here in this Tribunal, and the Prosecution's submission is that the real question for the Chamber is not the admissibility of this evidence but how much weight it should be given at the end of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you say you don't know the name of your source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the name of the man looking after the morgue at that time at the Kosevo hospital at that time, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very well. The evidence will be admitted and the weight to be attached to it will be considered at the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, you mentioned that this was the morgue at the Kosevo hospital. Did you ever see injured civilians being brought into the former military hospital from where you filmed the shelling of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Practically on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what kind of wounds did you observe on these civilians?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: A variety of wounds. We witnessed it, as well, at the casualty department of the Kosevo hospital; shrapnel wounds, bullet wounds. We also saw people coming in who were simply ill. But most of the casualties that came in to the hospital in those late afternoon and evening hours were people who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we can just finish, go to the end of this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the Prosecution would seek to tender this video material along with the English and B/C/S transcript, which is 65 ter number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That video clip is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P8, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. van Lynden, at some point, did you attempt to gain access to the area where the Bosnian Serb forces had their positions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: Yes, we did, both in June 1992 and again in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you eventually get access in September?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe how you obtained this access to the Bosnian Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: In June 1992, we had had a meeting in Pale, which was the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb political leadership, with Radovan Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you. Just for the record, who was Radovan Karadzic? What position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: He was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say "leader," are you referring to political, military --

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: The political leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: CAREL DIEDERIC AERNOUT VAN LYNDEN
utterances.text: But at that time, it was not possible to work up any kind of agreement that we could get such agreement.
